title: Atom
sentence: An atom is the basic unit of matter.

title: Atom
sentence: All normal matter – everything that has mass – is made of atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: This includes solids, liquids, and gases.

title: Atom
sentence: The atom cannot be broken to parts by chemistry, so people once thought it was the smallest and simplest particle of matter.

title: Atom
sentence: There are over 100 different kinds of atoms, called chemical elements.

title: Atom
sentence: Each kind has the same basic structure, but a different number of parts.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms are very small, but their exact size depends on the type.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms are from 0.1 to 0.5 nanometers across.

title: Atom
sentence: One nanometer is about 100,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair.

title: Atom
sentence: This makes one atom impossible to see without special tools.

title: Atom
sentence: Scientists learn how they work by doing experiments.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms are made of three kinds of subatomic particles.

title: Atom
sentence: These are protons, neutrons, and electrons.

title: Atom
sentence: Protons and neutrons have much more mass.

title: Atom
sentence: They are in the middle of the atom, the nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: Lightweight electrons move quickly around them.

title: Atom
sentence: The electromagnetic force holds the nucleus and electrons together.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same chemical element.

title: Atom
sentence: Examples of elements are carbon and gold.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms with the same number of protons, but different numbers of neutrons, are called isotopes.

title: Atom
sentence: Usually an atom has the same number of electrons as protons.

title: Atom
sentence: If an atom has more or less electrons than protons, it is called an ion, and has an electric charge.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms can join by chemical bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: Many things are made of more than one kind of atom.

title: Atom
sentence: These are chemical compounds or mixtures.

title: Atom
sentence: A group of atoms connected by chemical bonds is called a molecule.

title: Atom
sentence: For example, a water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

title: Atom
sentence: The forming or breaking of bonds is a chemical reaction.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms split if the forces inside are too weak to hold them together.

title: Atom
sentence: This is what causes radioactivity.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms can also join to make larger atoms at very high temperatures, such as inside a star.

title: Atom
sentence: These changes are studied in nuclear physics.

title: Atom
sentence: Most atoms on Earth are not radioactive.

title: Atom
sentence: They are rarely made, destroyed, or changed into another kind of atom.

title: Atom
sentence: The word "atom" comes from the Greek (ἀτόμος) "atomos", which means indivisible or uncuttable.

title: Atom
sentence: One of the first people to use the word "atom" is the Greek philosopher Democritus, around 400 BC.

title: Atom
sentence: He thought that everything was made of particles called atoms, which could not be divided into smaller pieces.

title: Atom
sentence: Some Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist philosophers also had ideas like this.

title: Atom
sentence: Atomic theory was a mostly philosophical subject, with not much scientific investigation or study, until the early 1800s.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1777 French chemist Antoine Lavoisier defined the term element as we now use it.

title: Atom
sentence: He said that an element was any substance that could not be broken down into other substances by the methods of chemistry.

title: Atom
sentence: Any substance which could be broken down was a compound.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1803, English philosopher John Dalton suggested that elements were made of tiny, solid balls called atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: Dalton believed that all atoms of the same element have the same mass.

title: Atom
sentence: He said that compounds are formed when atoms of more than one element combine.

title: Atom
sentence: In any one compound, the atoms would always combine in the same numbers.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1827, British scientist Robert Brown looked at pollen grains in water under his microscope.

title: Atom
sentence: The pollen grains appeared to be shaking.

title: Atom
sentence: Brown used Dalton's atomic theory to describe patterns in how they moved.

title: Atom
sentence: This was called Brownian motion.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1905 Albert Einstein used mathematics to prove that the pollen particles were being moved by the motion, or heat, of individual water molecules.

title: Atom
sentence: By doing this, he proved that atoms are real without question.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1869, Russian scientist Dmitri Mendeleev published the first periodic table.

title: Atom
sentence: The periodic table groups elements by their atomic number (how many protons they have; this is usually the same as the number of electrons).

title: Atom
sentence: Elements in the same column, or group, usually have similar qualities.

title: Atom
sentence: For example, helium, neon, argon, krypton, and xenon are all in the same column and are very similar.

title: Atom
sentence: All these elements are gases that have no color or smell.

title: Atom
sentence: Also, they cannot combine with other atoms to form compounds.

title: Atom
sentence: Together they are known as noble gases.

title: Atom
sentence: The physicist J.J. Thomson was the first person to discover electrons.

title: Atom
sentence: This happened while he was working with cathode rays in 1897.

title: Atom
sentence: He learned they had a negative charge, and the rest of the atom had a positive charge.

title: Atom
sentence: Thomson made the plum pudding model, which said that an atom was like plum pudding: the dried fruit (electrons) were stuck in a mass of pudding (having a positive charge).

title: Atom
sentence: In 1909, Ernest Rutherford used the Geiger–Marsden experiment to prove that most of an atom is in a very small space, the atomic nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: Rutherford took a photo plate and covered it with gold foil.

title: Atom
sentence: He then shot alpha particles (made of two protons and two neutrons stuck together) at it.

title: Atom
sentence: Many of the particles went through the gold foil, which proved that atoms are mostly empty space.

title: Atom
sentence: Electrons are so small and fast-moving that they did not block the particles from going through.

title: Atom
sentence: Rutherford later discovered protons in the nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1913, Niels Bohr created the Bohr model.

title: Atom
sentence: This model showed that electrons travel around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits.

title: Atom
sentence: This was better than the Rutherford model, but it was still not completely true.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1925, chemist Frederick Soddy discovered that some elements had more than one kind of atom, called isotopes.

title: Atom
sentence: Soddy believed that each different isotope of an element has a different mass.

title: Atom
sentence: To prove this, chemist Francis William Aston built the mass spectrometer, which measures the mass of single atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: Aston proved that Soddy was right.

title: Atom
sentence: He also found that the mass of each atom is a whole number times the mass of the proton.

title: Atom
sentence: This meant that there must be some particles in the nucleus other than protons.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1932, physicist James Chadwick shot alpha particles at beryllium atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: He saw that a particle shot out of the beryllium atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: This particle had no charge, but about the same mass as a proton.

title: Atom
sentence: He named this particle the neutron.

title: Atom
sentence: The best model so far comes from the Schrödinger equation.

title: Atom
sentence: Schrödinger learned that the electrons exist in a cloud around the nucleus, called the electron cloud.

title: Atom
sentence: In the electron cloud, it is impossible to know exactly where electrons are.

title: Atom
sentence: The Schrödinger equation says where an electron is likely to be.

title: Atom
sentence: This area is called the electron's orbital.

title: Atom
sentence: In 1937, German chemist Otto Hahn became the first person to make nuclear fission in a laboratory.

title: Atom
sentence: He discovered this by chance when shooting neutrons at a uranium atom, hoping to make a new isotope.

title: Atom
sentence: However, instead of a new isotope, the uranium changed into a barium atom, a smaller atom than uranium.

title: Atom
sentence: Hahn had "broken" the uranium atom.

title: Atom
sentence: This was the world's first recorded nuclear fission reaction.

title: Atom
sentence: This discovery led to the creation of the atomic bomb and nuclear power, where fission happens over and over again, creating a chain reaction.

title: Atom
sentence: Later in the 20th century, physicists went deeper into the mysteries of the atom.

title: Atom
sentence: Using particle accelerators, they discovered that protons and neutrons were made of other particles, called quarks.

title: Atom
sentence: An atom is made of three main particles: the proton, the neutron, and the electron.

title: Atom
sentence: Protons and neutrons have nearly the same size and mass (about  grams).

title: Atom
sentence: The mass of an electron is about 1800 times smaller (about  grams).

title: Atom
sentence: Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge.

title: Atom
sentence: Most atoms have no charge.

title: Atom
sentence: The number of protons (positive) and electrons (negative) are the same, so the charges balance out to zero.

title: Atom
sentence: However, ions have a different number of electrons than protons, so they have a positive or negative charge.

title: Atom
sentence: Scientists believe that electrons are elementary particles: they are not made of any smaller pieces.

title: Atom
sentence: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks of two kinds: up quarks and down quarks.

title: Atom
sentence: A proton is made of two up quarks and one down quark, and a neutron is made of two down quarks and one up quark.

title: Atom
sentence: The nucleus is in the middle of the atom.

title: Atom
sentence: It is made of protons and neutrons.

title: Atom
sentence: The nucleus makes up more than 99.9% of the mass of the atom.

title: Atom
sentence: However, it is very small: about 1 femtometer (10−15 m) across, which is around 100,000 times smaller than the width of an atom, so it has a very high density.

title: Atom
sentence: Usually in nature, two things with the same charge repel or shoot away from each other.

title: Atom
sentence: So for a long time, scientists did not know how the positively charged protons in the nucleus stayed together.

title: Atom
sentence: We now believe that the attraction between protons and neutrons comes from the strong nuclear force.

title: Atom
sentence: This force also holds together the quarks that make up the protons and neutrons.

title: Atom
sentence: Particles called mesons travel back and forth between protons and neutrons, and carry the force.

title: Atom
sentence: The number of neutrons in relation to protons defines whether the nucleus stays together or goes through radioactive decay.

title: Atom
sentence: When there are too many neutrons or protons, the atom tries to make the numbers smaller or more equal by removing the extra particles.

title: Atom
sentence: It sends out radiation in the form of alpha, beta, or gamma decay.

title: Atom
sentence: Nuclei can also change in other ways.

title: Atom
sentence: Nuclear fission is when the nucleus breaks into two smaller nuclei, releasing a lot of energy.

title: Atom
sentence: This release of energy makes nuclear fission useful for making bombs, and electricity in the form of nuclear power.

title: Atom
sentence: The other way nuclei can change is through nuclear fusion, when two nuclei join or fuse to make a larger nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: This process requires very high amounts of energy to overcome the electric repulsion between the protons, as they have the same charge.

title: Atom
sentence: Such high energies are most common in stars like our Sun, which fuses hydrogen for fuel.

title: Atom
sentence: However, once fusion happens, far more energy is released, because some of the mass becomes energy.

title: Atom
sentence: The energy needed to break a nucleus into protons and neutrons is called its nuclear binding energy.

title: Atom
sentence: This energy can be converted to mass, as stated by Einstein's famous formula E = mc2.

title: Atom
sentence: Medium-sized nuclei, such as iron-56 and nickel-62, have the highest binding energy per proton or neutron.

title: Atom
sentence: They will probably not go through fission or fusion, because they cannot release energy in this way.

title: Atom
sentence: Very small and very large atoms have low binding energy, so they are most willing to go through fission or fusion.

title: Atom
sentence: Electrons orbit, or travel around, the nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: They are called the atom's electron cloud.

title: Atom
sentence: They are attracted to the nucleus because of the electromagnetic force.

title: Atom
sentence: Electrons have a negative charge, and the nucleus always has a positive charge, so they attract each other.

title: Atom
sentence: The Bohr model shows that some electrons are farther from the nucleus than others in different levels.

title: Atom
sentence: These are called electron shells.

title: Atom
sentence: Only the electrons in the outer shell can make chemical bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: The number of electrons in the outer shell determines whether the atom is stable or which atoms it will bond with in a chemical reaction.

title: Atom
sentence: If an atom has only one shell, it needs two electrons to be complete.

title: Atom
sentence: Otherwise, the outer shell needs eight electrons to be complete.

title: Atom
sentence: The Bohr model is important because it has the idea of energy levels.

title: Atom
sentence: The electrons in each shell have a certain amount of energy.

title: Atom
sentence: Shells that are farther from the nucleus have more energy.

title: Atom
sentence: When a small burst of energy called a photon hits an electron, the electron can jump into a higher-energy shell.

title: Atom
sentence: This photon must carry exactly the right amount of energy to bring the electron to the new energy level.

title: Atom
sentence: A photon is a burst of light, and the amount of energy determines the color of light.

title: Atom
sentence: So each kind of atom will absorb certain colors of light, called the absorption spectrum.

title: Atom
sentence: An electron can also send out, or emit, a photon, and fall into a lower energy shell.

title: Atom
sentence: For the same reason, the atom will only send out certain colors of light, called the emission spectrum.

title: Atom
sentence: The complete picture is more complicated.

title: Atom
sentence: Unlike the Earth moving around the Sun, electrons do not move in a circle.

title: Atom
sentence: We cannot know the exact place of an electron.

title: Atom
sentence: We only know the probability, or chance, that it will be in any place.

title: Atom
sentence: Each electron is part of an orbital, which describes where it is likely to be.

title: Atom
sentence: No more than two electrons can be in one orbital; these two electrons have different spin.

title: Atom
sentence: In other words, it has 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second shell, and 7 in the third shell.

title: Atom
sentence: The number of protons in an atom is called its atomic number.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms of the same element have the same atomic number.

title: Atom
sentence: For example, all carbon atoms have six protons, so the atomic number of carbon is six.

title: Atom
sentence: Today, 118 elements are known.

title: Atom
sentence: Depending on how the number is counted, 90 to 94 elements exist naturally on earth.

title: Atom
sentence: All elements above number 94 have only been made by humans.

title: Atom
sentence: These elements are organized on the periodic table.

title: Atom
sentence: Because protons and neutrons have nearly the same mass, and the mass of electrons is very small, we can call the number of protons and neutrons in an atom its mass number.

title: Atom
sentence: Most elements have several isotopes with different mass numbers.

title: Atom
sentence: To name an isotope, we use the name of the element, followed by its mass number.

title: Atom
sentence: So an atom with six protons and seven neutrons is called carbon-13.

title: Atom
sentence: Sometimes, we need a more exact measurement.

title: Atom
sentence: The exact mass of an atom is called its atomic mass.

title: Atom
sentence: This is usually measured with the atomic mass unit (amu), also called the dalton.

title: Atom
sentence: One amu is exactly 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, which is  grams.

title: Atom
sentence: Hydrogen-1 has a mass of about 1 amu.

title: Atom
sentence: The heaviest atom known, oganesson, has a mass of about 294 amu, or  grams.

title: Atom
sentence: The average mass of all atoms of a particular element is called its atomic weight.

title: Atom
sentence: The size of an atom depends on the size of its electron cloud.

title: Atom
sentence: Moving down the periodic table, more electron shells are added.

title: Atom
sentence: As a result, atoms get bigger.

title: Atom
sentence: Moving to the right on the periodic table, more protons are added to the nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: This more positive nucleus pulls electrons more strongly, so atoms get smaller.

title: Atom
sentence: The biggest atom is caesium, which is about 0.596 nanometers wide according to one model.

title: Atom
sentence: The smallest atom is helium, which is about 0.062 nanometers wide.

title: Atom
sentence: When atoms are far apart, they attract each other.

title: Atom
sentence: This attraction is stronger for some kinds of atoms than others.

title: Atom
sentence: At the same time, the heat, or kinetic energy, of atoms makes them always move.

title: Atom
sentence: If the attraction is strong enough, relative to the amount of heat, atoms will form a solid.

title: Atom
sentence: If the attraction is weaker, they will form a liquid, and if it is even weaker, they will form a gas.

title: Atom
sentence: Chemical bonds are the strongest kinds of attraction between atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: The movement of electrons explains all chemical bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms usually bond with each other in a way that fills or empties their outer electron shell.

title: Atom
sentence: The most reactive elements have an almost full or almost empty outer shell.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms with a full outer shell, called noble gases, do not usually form bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: There are three main kinds of bonds: ionic bonds, covalent bonds, and metallic bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: In an ionic bond, one atom gives electrons to another atom.

title: Atom
sentence: Each atom becomes an ion: an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.

title: Atom
sentence: The positive ion (which has lost electrons) is called a cation; it is usually a metal.

title: Atom
sentence: The negative ion (which has gained electrons) is called an anion; it is usually a nonmetal.

title: Atom
sentence: Ionic bonding usually results in a regular network, or crystal, of ions held together.

title: Atom
sentence: In a covalent bond, two atoms share electrons.

title: Atom
sentence: This usually happens when both atoms are nonmetals.

title: Atom
sentence: Covalent bonds often form molecules, ranging in size from two atoms to many more.

title: Atom
sentence: They can also form large networks, such as glass or graphite.

title: Atom
sentence: The number of bonds that an atom makes (its valency) is usually the number of electrons needed to fill its outer electron shell.

title: Atom
sentence: In a metallic bond, electrons travel freely between many metal atoms.

title: Atom
sentence: Any number of atoms can bond this way.

title: Atom
sentence: Metals conduct electric current because electric charge can easily flow through them.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms in metals can move past each other, so it is easy to bend, stretch, and change the shape of metals.

title: Atom
sentence: All atoms attract each other by Van der Waals forces.

title: Atom
sentence: These forces are weaker than chemical bonds.

title: Atom
sentence: They are caused when electrons move to one side of an atom.

title: Atom
sentence: This movement gives a negative charge to that side.

title: Atom
sentence: It also gives a positive charge to the other side.

title: Atom
sentence: When two atoms line up their sides with negative and positive charges, they will attract.

title: Atom
sentence: Although atoms are mostly empty space, they cannot pass through each other.

title: Atom
sentence: When two atoms are very close, their electron clouds will repel each other by the electromagnetic force.

title: Atom
sentence: To understand how magnets work, we can look at the properties of the atom.

title: Atom
sentence: Any magnet has a north and south pole, and a certain strength.

title: Atom
sentence: The direction and strength of a magnet, together, are called its magnetic moment.

title: Atom
sentence: Every electron also has a magnetic moment, like a tiny magnet.

title: Atom
sentence: This comes from the electron's spin and its orbit around the nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: The magnetic moments for the electrons add up to a magnetic moment for the whole atom.

title: Atom
sentence: This tells us how atoms act in a magnetic field.

title: Atom
sentence: Every electron has one of two opposite spins.

title: Atom
sentence: We can think of one as turning to the right, and the other as turning to the left.

title: Atom
sentence: If every electron is paired with an electron with the opposite spin in the same orbital, the magnetic moments will cancel out to zero.

title: Atom
sentence: Atoms like this are called diamagnetic.

title: Atom
sentence: They are only weakly repelled by a magnetic field.

title: Atom
sentence: However, if some electrons are not paired, the atom will have a lasting magnetic moment: it will be paramagnetic or ferromagnetic.

title: Atom
sentence: When atoms are paramagnetic, the magnetic moment of each atom points in a random direction.

title: Atom
sentence: They are weakly attracted to a magnetic field.

title: Atom
sentence: When atoms are ferromagnetic, the magnetic moments of nearby atoms act on each other.

title: Atom
sentence: They point in the same direction.

title: Atom
sentence: This means that the whole object is a magnet, and it can point in the direction of a magnetic field.

title: Atom
sentence: Ferromagnetic materials, such as iron, cobalt, and nickel, are strongly attracted to a magnetic field.

title: Atom
sentence: Some elements, and many isotopes, have what is called an unstable nucleus.

title: Atom
sentence: This means the nucleus is either too big to hold itself together, or it has too many protons or neutrons.

title: Atom
sentence: When a nucleus is unstable, it has to eliminate the excess mass of particles.

title: Atom
sentence: It does this through radiation.

title: Atom
sentence: An atom that does this is called radioactive.

title: Atom
sentence: Unstable atoms emit radiation until they lose enough particles in the nucleus to become stable.

title: Atom
sentence: All atoms above atomic number 82 (82 protons, lead) are radioactive.

title: Atom
sentence: There are three main kinds of radioactive decay: alpha, beta, and gamma.

title: Atom
sentence: Alpha decay is when the atom shoots out a particle having two protons and two neutrons.

title: Atom

sentence: Since then, people have collected and studied statistics on many things.

title: Statistics
sentence: Trees, starfish, stars, rocks, words, almost anything that can be counted has been a subject of statistics.

title: Statistics
sentence: Before we can describe the world with statistics, we must collect data.

title: Statistics
sentence: The data that we collect in statistics are called measurements.

title: Statistics
sentence: After we collect data, we use one or more numbers to describe each observation or measurement.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, suppose that we want to find out how popular a certain TV show is.

title: Statistics
sentence: We can pick a group of people (called a sample) out of the total population of viewers.

title: Statistics
sentence: Then we ask each viewer in the sample how often they watch the show.

title: Statistics
sentence: The sample is data that one can see, and the population is data that one cannot see (assuming that not every viewer in the population are asked).

title: Statistics
sentence: For another example, if we want to know whether a certain drug can help lower blood pressure, we could give the drug to people for some time and measure their blood pressure before and after.

title: Statistics
sentence: Numbers that describe the data one can see are called descriptive statistics.

title: Statistics
sentence: Numbers that make predictions about the data one cannot see are called inferential statistics.

title: Statistics
sentence: Descriptive statistics involves using numbers to describe features of data.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, the average height of women in the United States is a descriptive statistic: it describes a feature (average height) of a population (women in the United States).

title: Statistics
sentence: Once the results have been summarized and described, they can be used for prediction.

title: Statistics
sentence: This is called inferential statistics.

title: Statistics
sentence: As an example, the size of an animal is dependent on many factors.

title: Statistics
sentence: Some of these factors are controlled by the environment, but others are by inheritance.

title: Statistics
sentence: A biologist might therefore make a model that says that there is a high probability that the offspring will be small in size—if the parents were small in size.

title: Statistics
sentence: This model probably allows to predict the size in better ways than by just guessing at random.

title: Statistics
sentence: Testing whether a certain drug can be used to cure a certain condition or disease is usually done by comparing the results of people who are given the drug against those who are given a placebo.

title: Statistics
sentence: Most often, we collect statistical data by doing surveys or experiments.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, an opinion poll is one kind of survey.

title: Statistics
sentence: We pick a small number of people and ask them questions.

title: Statistics
sentence: Then, we use their answers as the data.

title: Statistics
sentence: The choice of which individuals to take for a survey or data collection is important, as it directly influences the statistics.

title: Statistics
sentence: When the statistics are done, it can no longer be determined which individuals are taken.

title: Statistics
sentence: Suppose we want to measure the water quality of a big lake.

title: Statistics
sentence: If we take samples next to the waste drain, we will get different results than if the samples are taken in a far-away and hard-to-reach spot of the lake.

title: Statistics
sentence: If there are many samples, the samples will likely be very close to what they are in the real population.

title: Statistics
sentence: If there are very few samples, however, they might be very different from what they are in the real population.

title: Statistics
sentence: This error is called a chance error (see also Errors and residuals in statistics).

title: Statistics
sentence: The individuals for the samples need to be chosen carefully.

title: Statistics
sentence: Usually, they will be chosen randomly.

title: Statistics
sentence: If this is not the case, the samples might be very different from what they really are in the total population.

title: Statistics
sentence: This is true even if a great number of samples is taken.

title: Statistics
sentence: This kind of error is called bias.

title: Statistics
sentence: We can reduce chance errors by taking a larger sample, and we can avoid some bias by choosing randomly.

title: Statistics
sentence: However, sometimes large random samples are hard to take.

title: Statistics
sentence: And bias can happen if different people are not asked, or refuse to answer our questions, or if they know they are getting a fake treatment.

title: Statistics
sentence: These problems can be hard to fix.

title: Statistics
sentence: See standard error for more.

title: Statistics
sentence: The middle of the data is called an average.

title: Statistics
sentence: The average tells us about a typical individual in the population.

title: Statistics
sentence: There are three kinds of average that are often used: the mean, the median and the mode.

title: Statistics
sentence: Where  are the data and  is the population size (see also Sigma Notation).

title: Statistics
sentence: The problem with the mean is that it does not tell anything about how the values are distributed.

title: Statistics
sentence: Values that are very large or very small change the mean a lot.

title: Statistics
sentence: In statistics, these extreme values might be errors of measurement, but sometimes the population really does contain these values.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, if there are 10 people in a room who make $10 per day and 1 who makes $1,000,000 per day.

title: Statistics
sentence: The mean of the data is $90,918 per day.

title: Statistics
sentence: Even though it is the average amount, the mean in this case is not the amount any single person makes, and thus is not very useful for some purposes.

title: Statistics
sentence: The mean described above is the "arithmetic mean".

title: Statistics
sentence: Other kinds are useful for some purposes.

title: Statistics
sentence: The median is the middle item of the data.

title: Statistics
sentence: For a given data , this is sometimes written as .

title: Statistics
sentence: To find the median, we sort the data from the smallest number to the largest number, and then choose the number in the middle.

title: Statistics
sentence: If there is an even number of data, there will not be a number right in the middle, so we choose the two middle ones and calculate their mean.

title: Statistics
sentence: In our example above, there are 10 items of data, the two middle ones are "57" and "64", so the median is (57+64)/2 = 60.5.

title: Statistics
sentence: As another example, like the income example presented for the mean, consider a room with 10 people who have incomes of $10, $20, $20, $40, $50, $60, $90, $90, $100, and $1,000,000.

title: Statistics
sentence: Here, the median is $55, because $55 is the average of the two middle numbers, $50 and $60.

title: Statistics
sentence: If the extreme value of $1,000,000 is ignored, the mean is $53.

title: Statistics
sentence: In this case, the median is close to the value obtained when the extreme value is thrown out.

title: Statistics
sentence: The median solves the problem of extreme values as described in the definition of mean above.

title: Statistics
sentence: The mode is the most frequent item of data.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, the most common letter in English is the letter "e".

title: Statistics
sentence: We would say that "e" is the mode of the distribution of the letters.

title: Statistics
sentence: As another example, if there are 10 people in a room with incomes of $10, $20, $20, $40, $50, $60, $90, $90, $90, $100, and $1,000,000, then the mode is $90, because $90 occurs three times and all other values occur fewer than three times.

title: Statistics
sentence: There can be more than one mode.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, if there are 10 people in a room with incomes of $10, $20, $20, $20, $50, $60, $90, $90, $90, $100, and $1,000,000, the modes are $20 and $90.

title: Statistics
sentence: This is bi-modal, or has two modes.

title: Statistics
sentence: Bi-modality is very common, and it often indicates that the data is the combination of two different groups.

title: Statistics
sentence: For instance, the average height of all adults in the U.S. has a bi-modal distribution.

title: Statistics
sentence: This is because males and females have separate average heights of 1.763 m (5 ft 9 + 1⁄2 in) for men and 1.622 m (5 ft 4 in) for women.

title: Statistics
sentence: These peaks are apparent when both groups are combined.

title: Statistics
sentence: The mode is the only form of average that can be used for data that can not be put in order.

title: Statistics
sentence: Another thing we can say about a set of data is how spread out it is.

title: Statistics
sentence: A common way to describe the spread of a set of data is the standard deviation.

title: Statistics
sentence: If the standard deviation of a set of data is small, then most of the data is very close to the average.

title: Statistics
sentence: If the standard deviation is large, though, then a lot of the data is very different from the average.

title: Statistics
sentence: The standard deviation of a sample is generally different from the standard deviation of its originating population .

title: Statistics
sentence: Because of that, we write  for population standard deviation, and  for sample standard deviation.

title: Statistics
sentence: If the data follows the common pattern called the normal distribution, then it is very useful to know the standard deviation.

title: Statistics
sentence: If the data follows this pattern (we would say the data is normally distributed), about 68 of every 100 pieces of data will be off the average by less than the standard deviation.

title: Statistics
sentence: Not only that, but about 95 of every 100 measurements will be off the average by less than two times the standard deviation, and about 997 in 1000 will be closer to the average by less than three standard deviations.

title: Statistics
sentence: We also can use statistics to find out that some percent, percentile, number, or fraction of people or things in a group do something or fit in a certain category.

title: Statistics
sentence: For example, social scientists used statistics to find out that 49% of people in the world are males.

title: Speed
sentence: It is velocity but without the direction.

title: Speed
sentence: Speed is the distance an object moves in a given amount of time.

title: Speed
sentence: If a train takes 1 hour to travel 100 kilometers, it has a speed of .

title: Speed
sentence: In fact this is the average speed.

title: Speed
sentence: During this one hour, the train may become slower and faster, it may even drive backwards.

title: Speed
sentence: The average speed of an object in a certain time is the distance the object traveled divided by the time.

title: Speed
sentence: The instantaneous speed is the average speed when the time is very small, almost zero.

title: Speed
sentence: There are many units of measurement.

title: Speed
sentence: Different units are used for different applications.

title: Speed
sentence: People controlling planes and ships frequently use Knot (speed).

title: Speed
sentence: Sometimes a Mach number is used.

title: Speed
sentence: A “negative speed” would be in fact a velocity.

title: Speed
sentence: The biggest speed is the speed of light.

title: Speed
sentence: You can write bigger speeds, but they are not possible in this universe.

title: Server
sentence: In net jargon, a server is a computer that serves many kinds of information to a user or client machine.

title: Server
sentence: Usually a server will only do a few things for many clients.

title: Server
sentence: Every type of thing a server does is called a service.

title: Server
sentence: Services are used by other computers that are called clients.

title: Server
sentence: The relationship between client and server is called a client-server relationship.

title: Server
sentence: For example, Wikipedia has web servers which have a service for sending web pages over the Internet.

title: Server
sentence: Your client computer talks to Wikipedia's web page service to get web pages for you.

title: Server
sentence: A server can also host internet games, share files, and give access to peripheral equipment such as printers.

title: Server
sentence: In simple words, the individual computers are connected to some powerful computers called servers.

title: Server
sentence: These store files and information in the form of website.

title: Server
sentence: With an Internet connection, different users anywhere in the world can access these files.

title: Server
sentence: For servers and clients to talk to each other, they need to be connected to a network.

title: Server
sentence: They need to use the same communication protocol, a set way for machines to talk to other machines.

title: Server
sentence: It is like a language.

title: Server
sentence: For example, the Wikipedia server runs the HTTP to send web sites to your computer, and your computer uses the HTTP Protocol to ask Wikipedia for pages.

title: Server
sentence: Usually, servers are specially made to be more powerful and reliable.

title: Server
sentence: They are usually more expensive than normal computers.

title: Server
sentence: Sometimes, servers can be clustered, which means many servers are working together to do one service.

title: Server
sentence: The server might slow down if there are too many people accessing the server at the same time, resulting in a high load.

title: Server
sentence: An overloaded server might also shut itself down automatically.

title: Server
sentence: In a peer-to-peer system, every computer is both a client and a server to the others.

title: Server
sentence: This is commonly put into file sharing and VOIP.

title: Server
sentence: However, this can help in attempts at piracy.

title: Server
sentence: Typical server operating systems are Linux, FreeBSD, NetBSD, and OpenBSD.

title: Server
sentence: Unlike other computers, a server often has no monitor, keyboard, or mouse.

title: Server
sentence: When a server doesn't have to do very much, server software can run on a computer that is also doing other things.Initially, such servers were connected to clients known as terminals that did not do any actual computing.

title: Server
sentence: These terminals, referred to as dumb terminals, existed simply to accept input via a keyboard or card reader and to return the results of any computations to a display screen or printer.

title: Server
sentence: The actual computing was done on the server.

title: Server
sentence: Servers also have a special ip number that other devices use to find the servers.

title: Server
sentence: A web server is a type of server that is used to host websites.

title: Server
sentence: Examples of web server software include Apache or IIS.

title: Server
sentence: A web server can host one, or many, websites.

title: Server
sentence: The default port for a web server to listen to is port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS).

title: Server
sentence: Some web servers do other things than just serving a web page.

title: Server
sentence: For example, they may have something called SSI that makes building a website easier.

title: Server
sentence: Web servers use services like CGI to let software on the server make web pages.

title: Server
sentence: Some of the programming languages that can use CGI are scripting languages like Perl, Python, PHP, or ASP.

title: Server
sentence: Some are compiled languages like C++ or Java.

title: Simile
sentence: A simile is a figure of speech that compares two different things, usually by using the words 'like' or 'as'.

title: Simile
sentence: It is used to make a direct and clear comparison between two things .Similes may be confused with metaphors, which do the same kind of thing.

title: Simile
sentence: Similes use comparisons, with the words 'like' or 'as'.

title: Simile
sentence: Metaphors use indirect comparisons, without the words 'like' or 'as'.

title: Simile
sentence: Like a hungry wolf, he ate the food.

title: Simile
sentence: A dragonfly is like a plane: they both fly and cannot close their wings.

title: Simile
sentence: The color yellow is like walking into a surprise birthday party.

title: Simile
sentence: He talks about similes.

title: State
sentence: A people, the population of the state.

title: State
sentence: Institutions which have the power to make laws.

title: State
sentence: There are different forms of government a state may have, for example a republic or a monarchy.

title: State
sentence: Sometimes states form their own countries.

title: State
sentence: In its origin the United States had different kinds of states, but they agreed to join together.

title: State
sentence: Most states also have armed forces, civil service, law and police.

title: State
sentence: Government institutions in a country are commonly referred to as "the state".

title: State
sentence: Max Weber (1864-1920) had another definition: According to him, a state is a community of people which has "the monopoly to legitimately use physical force within a well-defined area".

title: State
sentence: Another definition  is from political science: A state is a system of public institutions which are there to regulate the  issues of a society.

title: State
sentence: Some philiospohers, such as Aristotle, Rousseau and Hegel had a moralistic view: In their opinion, a state arises when individuals reach their goals and that of society.

title: State
sentence: According to Hegel,  the state is the reason God came into the world; it is the power of reason.

title: State
sentence: This reason manifests as His will.

title: State
sentence: Because of the different definitions, there's no universally accepted definition of state.

title: State
sentence: The one given at the start of the article is now part of international law.

title: State
sentence: The earliest states could not be just human settlements.

title: State
sentence: They had to be more than tribes.

title: State
sentence: An example is New Guinea, which has many small tribes, but no larger organisations.

title: State
sentence: Amazonia in the 18th century was also like this, with many small tribes.

title: State
sentence: They are not states.

title: State
sentence: To be a state, tribes have to be bounded together, for example, by a monarch.

title: State
sentence: They may also be bonded by their language, and by living in the same region.

title: State
sentence: An example of monarchy is early Egypt under the Pharaohs.

title: State
sentence: Similar military-based states included the Babylonian Empire and the huge Roman Empire and early China.

title: State
sentence: Some early states were based on cities.

title: State
sentence: Some Ancient Greek city-states had democracy in a limited form.

title: State
sentence: Other states had inheritance of kingship or even challenges and fighting to decide leadership.

title: State
sentence: Early city states had a feature that modern society cannot match.

title: State
sentence: Every man got to see and know the leading citizens.

title: State
sentence: One reason was that the adult men would do the fighting if the group were attacked.

title: State
sentence: When the military-based state, the Roman Empire, fell, lots of little states were made and each was also military-based and controlled by a king.

title: State
sentence: These states did not often work together and war raged.

title: State
sentence: However, once people within the state itself started fighting (what's called a Civil war), the kings had to make peace and start parliaments.

title: State
sentence: These states all tried to improve their politics and economy.

title: State
sentence: They became more and more like the states today.

title: State
sentence: They formed proper boundaries for their lands and worked with the powers in the state, such as the Church and the nobility.

title: State
sentence: They made armies, tax systems and embassies to make them more powerful and stable.

title: State
sentence: Types of state can be separated into two categories: democracy and dictatorship.

title: State
sentence: However, just because a group of states are all democratic does not mean that they follow the same rules.

title: State
sentence: Iran, Pakistan, France, Germany and the United States of America are all states.

title: State
sentence: Each of them sees itself as a democracy.

title: State
sentence: Each of them however has a different idea of what democracy really means.

title: State
sentence: Different states of the same 'category' can also function differently.

title: State
sentence: For example, two democratic states may be quite different if one has a well-trained police or army while the other does not.

title: State
sentence: Therefore, the word 'state' only tells us what type of government that state follows (democratic or dictatorship) and does not tell us about the country itself.

title: State
sentence: There are lots of sub-types of state branching off from democracy and dictatorship.

title: State
sentence: The main ones are Pluralism, Marxism and Institutionalism.

title: State
sentence: Pluralism has been very popular in the United States.

title: State
sentence: It shows the state as a neutral place for settling arguments between other states.

title: State
sentence: Pluralism allows each group of people to tell the state what to do.

title: State
sentence: This type of state is called a polyarchy.

title: State
sentence: Also in a pluralist state, politics, the military and the economy are all united and work together.

title: State
sentence: This means that all power in the state is 'diffused' across the people who live there.

title: State
sentence: Marxism is an ideology advocating for the rights of workers and labourers of society.

title: State
sentence: It was started by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.

title: State
sentence: Marxism rejects the idea that a state is there to protect business interest, and is definitely not a neutral place for settling arguments.

title: State
sentence: The main job of a Marxist state is to protect the labour and financial situation of the working classes.

title: State
sentence: With such reforms, a Marxist state focuses on collectivising resources and creating a planned economy to ensure the well-being of the workers.

title: State
sentence: Both Marxist and Pluralist states have to react to the activities of groups of people in the state itself.

title: State
sentence: Institutionalist states do not see themselves as 'instruments' to be controlled, they are more just geographical areas.

title: State
sentence: In this area, the people just form groups themselves.

title: State
sentence: An institutionalist state can be made up of both Marxist and Pluralist people, both which have the power to control themselves and not influence the other parties of the state.

title: State
sentence: Anarchism is when a group of people have complete freedom and do not believe in having a state at all.

title: State
sentence: Anarchists are a lot like Marxists, but they believe (opposite to Marxists) that a country can work without without a state forcing people to do anything.

title: State
sentence: Law and order are not necessary.

title: State
sentence: Anarchists (such as Bakunin and Kropotkin in the 19th century), often want a form of Marxism but ignoring some of their rules.

title: State
sentence: They want workers to manage themselves and simply get paid for what they do, rather than getting paid in wages.

title: Stream
sentence: A stream is a natural flow of water moving across land between banks.

title: Stream
sentence: It is smaller than a river.

title: Stream
sentence: The primary meaning of stream is a body of water, confined within a bed and banks, and detectably flowing.

title: Stream
sentence: Synonyms or related words include river, creek, tributary, run, branch, brook, bourne, wash, and fork.

title: Stream
sentence: Navigable streams are sometimes called waterways, though the term may apply to any size of permanent and natural water feature except oceans.

title: Stream
sentence: In the United States, an intermittent stream is one that only flows for part of the year and is marked on topographic maps with a line of blue dashes and dots.

title: Stream
sentence: In desert areas of the American Southwest, this also includes washes, which only flow after thunderstorms or other significant rains.

title: Stream
sentence: A blue-line stream is one which flows for most or all of the year and is marked on topographic maps with a solid blue line.

title: Stream
sentence: In Australia, an intermittent stream is usually called a creek, and marked on topographic maps with a solid blue line.

title: Stream
sentence: Generally, streams that form only during and immediately after precipitation are termed ephemeral streams.

title: Stream
sentence: Streams in geographic terms are awarded order designations.

title: Stream
sentence: A stream of the first order is a blue-line stream which does not have any other blue-line stream feeding into it.

title: Stream
sentence: A stream of the second order is one which is formed by the joining of two or more blue-line streams.

title: Stream
sentence: A third-order stream is one below the confluence of two or more second-order streams; a fourth-order stream is formed by the confluence of at least two third-order streams, and so forth.

title: Stream
sentence: Typically, streams are said to have a particular profile, beginning with steep gradients, no flood plain, and little shifting of channels, eventually evolving into streams with low gradients, wide flood plains, and extensive meanders.

title: Stream
sentence: The initial stage is sometimes termed a "young" stream, and the later state a "mature" or "old" stream.

title: Stream
sentence: However, a stream may meander for some distance before falling into a "young" stream condition.

title: Stream
sentence: The gradient of a stream is a critical factor in determining its character, and is entirely determined by its base level of erosion.

title: Stream
sentence: The base level of erosion is the point at which the stream either enters the ocean, a lake or pond, or enters a stretch in which it has a much lower gradient, and may be specifically applied to any particular stretch of a stream.

title: Stream
sentence: In geologic terms, the stream will erode down through its bed to achieve the base level of erosion throughout its course.

title: Stream
sentence: If this base level is low, then the stream will rapidly cut through underlying strata and have a steep gradient, and if the base level is relatively high, then the stream will form a flood plain and meanders.

title: Stream
sentence: When a stream flows over an especially resistant stratum and forms a waterfall or cascade, or the same results because for some reason the base level of erosion suddenly drops, perhaps as a result of a fault, the resulting sudden change in stream elevation is called a nickpoint.

title: Stream
sentence: The stream, of course, expends kinetic energy in "trying" to eliminate the nickpoint.

title: Stream
sentence: Meanders are looping changes of direction of a stream.

title: Stream
sentence: These may be somewhat sine-wave in form.

title: Stream
sentence: Typically, over time, the meanders don't disappear but gradually migrate downstream.

title: Stream
sentence: However, if some resistant material slows or stops the downstream movement of a meander, a stream may erode through the neck between two legs of a meander to become temporarily straighter, leaving behind an arc-shaped body of water termed an oxbow lake or bayou.

title: Stream
sentence: A flood may also result in a meander being cut through in this way.

title: Stream
sentence: The point of origin of a stream is often called the headwaters or source.

title: Stream
sentence: The entire basin drained by the stream is termed the watershed.

title: Stream
sentence: Every watershed is made up of smaller watersheds, while most watersheds are parts of larger watersheds.

title: Stream
sentence: For instance, the Continental Divide in North America divides the Atlantic Ocean watershed from the Pacific Ocean watershed, but the Atlantic Ocean watershed may be first divided into the Atlantic Ocean drainage and the Gulf of Mexico drainage.

title: Stream
sentence: This delineation within the United States is termed the Eastern Divide.

title: Stream
sentence: The Gulf of Mexico watershed may be divided into Mississippi River basin and a number of smaller watersheds, such as the Tombigbee River watershed.

title: Stream
sentence: The Mississippi River watershed includes the Ohio River watershed, which in turn includes the Kentucky River watershed, and so forth.

title: Stream
sentence: The point at which a stream empties into an ocean or other large body of relatively level water is termed the mouth.

title: Stream
sentence: There may often be an estuary or delta at the mouth.

title: Stream
sentence: Some streams flow underground through unconsolidated sediments or through caves.

title: Stream
sentence: Especially with caves, a stream may flow aboveground for part of its course, and underground for part of its course.

title: Stream
sentence: When a stream emerges from an underground course, it is termed a spring.

title: Stream
sentence: The study of streams and waterways in general is known as surface hydrology and is important in environmental geography or environmental geology.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Solar System is the Sun and all the objects that orbit around it.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Sun is orbited by planets, asteroids, comets and other things.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Solar System is about 4.568 billion years old.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Sun formed by gravity in a large molecular cloud.

title: Solar System
sentence: It is mainly hydrogen, which it converts into helium through nuclear fusion.

title: Solar System
sentence: The planets are in a flattened orbiting disk.

title: Solar System
sentence: This disk was left over from the cloud that formed the Sun.

title: Solar System
sentence: Eventually, the gas and dust of the disk came together into planets.

title: Solar System
sentence: It is thought that almost all stars and their planets form this way.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Sun is a star.

title: Solar System
sentence: It makes up 99.9% of the Solar System's mass.

title: Solar System
sentence: This means that it has strong gravity.

title: Solar System
sentence: The other objects are pulled into orbit around the Sun.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Sun is mostly made out of hydrogen, and some helium and higher elements.

title: Solar System
sentence: All heavier elements, called metals in astronomy, account for less than 2% of the Sun's mass.

title: Solar System
sentence: Oxygen is about 1% of the Sun's mass.

title: Solar System
sentence: Iron (0.2%) is the most plentiful of the other elements.

title: Solar System
sentence: There are eight planets in the Solar System.

title: Solar System
sentence: From closest to farthest from the Sun, they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

title: Solar System
sentence: The first four planets are called terrestrial planets.

title: Solar System
sentence: They are mostly made of rock and metal, and they are mostly solid.

title: Solar System
sentence: The last four planets are called gas giants.

title: Solar System
sentence: This is because they are much larger than other planets and are mostly made of gas.

title: Solar System
sentence: Six of the planets, and the six largest dwarf planets, are orbited by moons.

title: Solar System
sentence: There are more than 200 moons in the Solar System.

title: Solar System
sentence: Mercury and Venus have no moons, and Jupiter and Saturn have the largest number of moons.

title: Solar System
sentence: The largest moon is Ganymede which is a moon of Jupiter.

title: Solar System
sentence: Titan is one of Saturn’s moons.

title: Solar System
sentence: It is the only moon in the Solar System to have an atmosphere, which is mainly composed of nitrogen.

title: Solar System
sentence: The Solar System also contains other things.

title: Solar System
sentence: There are asteroid belts, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.

title: Solar System
sentence: Further out than Neptune, there is the Kuiper belt and the scattered disc.

title: Solar System
sentence: These areas have dwarf planets, including Pluto, Makemake, Haumea, Ceres and Eris.

title: Solar System
sentence: There are thousands of very small objects in these areas.

title: Solar System

Zero (0) is a special number.
If there are zero things, then there is nothing at all.
For example, if a person has zero hats, that means they do not have any hats.
The symbol for the number zero is "0".
It is the additive identity of common numbers.
This means that if a number is added to 0, then that number would remain unchanged.

The idea of zero was first thought about in Babylon, India and in Central America at different times.
Some places and countries did not know about zero, which may have made it harder for those people to do mathematics.
For example, the year after 1 BC is AD 1 (there is no year zero).
In India, zero was theorized in the seventh century by the :Mathematician  :Aryabhata.
Over hundreds of years, the idea of zero was passed from country to country, from India and Babylon to other places, like Greece, Persia and the Arab world.
The Europeans learned about zero from the Arabs, and stopped using Roman math.
This is why numbers are called "Arabic numerals".
Zero is almost never used as a place number (ordinal number).
This means that it is not used like 1, 2, or 3 to indicate the order, or place, of something, like 1st, 2nd, or 3rd.
An exception to this is seen in many programming languages.
The number zero is a whole number (counting number).
The number zero is not a positive number.
The number zero is not a negative number, either.
The number zero is a neutral number.
In time, zero means "now".
For example, when a person is counting down the time to the start of something, such as a foot race or when a rocket takes off, the count is: "three, two, one, zero (or go)".
Zero is the exact time of the start of the race or when the rocket takes off into the sky.
In most (if not all) numerical systems, 0 was identified before the idea of 'negative integers' was accepted.
It means "courageous one" in hieroglyphics.

Zero is a number which means an amount of null size; that is, if the number of brothers is zero, that means the same thing as having no brothers, and if something has a weight of zero, it has no weight.
If the difference between the numbers of pieces in two piles is zero, it means the two piles have an equal number of pieces.
Before counting starts, the result can be assumed to be zero; that is the number of items counted before one counts the first item, and counting the first item brings the result to one.
And if there are no items to be counted, zero remains the final result.
While mathematicians all accept zero as a number, some non-mathematicians would say that zero is not a number, arguing that one cannot have zero of something.
Others say that if one has a bank balance of zero, one has a specific quantity of money in that account, namely none.
It is that latter view which is accepted by mathematicians and most others.
Is zero a natural number ?
A debate asking if 0 is or not a natural number has been discussed over time.
Encyclopædia Britannica says 0 is a natural number.
Wolfram MathWorld´says it isn't.
The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences says it isn't.
The Princeton Companion to Mathematics says 0 is a natural number.
Although the International Baccalaureate thinks 0 to be a natural number.
Oxford Dictionary says "a positive whole number such as 1, 2, or 3, and sometimes also zero".
There was no year zero between 1 BC and 1 AD.

More specifically, almost all historians leave out the year zero from the proleptic Gregorian and Julian calendars (that is, from the normal calendar used in English-speaking countries), but astronomers include it in these same calendars.
However, the phrase Year Zero may be used to describe any event considered so important, that someone might want to start counting years all over again from zero.

The four-segment 0 is not common.
The number zero (as in the "zero brothers" example above) is not the same as the numeral or digit zero, used in numeral systems using positional notation.
Successive positions of digits have higher values, so the digit zero is used to skip a position and give appropriate value to the preceding and following digits.
A zero digit is not always necessary in a different positional number system.
Something called bijective numeration is a possible example of a system without zeroes.
It is used to hold the place of that digit, because correct placing of digits affects a numeral's value.

The number 0 and the letter O are both round, though of different widths.
The difference is important on a computer.
For one thing, a computer will not do arithmetic with the letter O, because it does not know that it should have been a zero.
The oval-shaped zero and circular letter O came into use together on modern character displays.
The zero with a dot in the centre seems to have begun as a choice on IBM 3270 controllers (this has the problem that it looks like the Greek letter theta).

This format causes problems because it looks like the symbol , representing the empty set, as well as for certain Scandinavian languages which use Ø as a letter.

The rule which has the letter O with a slash and the zero without was used at IBM and a few other early mainframe makers; this is even more of a problem for Scandinavians, because it looks like two of their letters at the same time.
Some Burroughs/Unisys computers display a zero with a backwards slash.

And yet another convention common on early line printers left zero without any extra dots or slashes but added a tail or hook to the letter O so that it resembled an inverted Q or cursive capital letter O.

Zeroes of a function are used because they are another way to talk about solving an equation, which is a main goal in algebra.
If we want to solve an equation like x2 = 1, then we can subtract the right-hand side of the equation from both sides, in this case 1.
Whatever we get on the left-hand side, in this case x2 − 1, can be called a function  f(x).
The right-hand side has to be zero, because we subtracted it from itself.
Finding the zeroes of this function is the same as solving this equation.

We got this equation by subtracting the same thing from both sides, so we also have solutions to the equation we started with, in this case x2 = 1.
More generally, if we could find zeroes of functions, we could solve any equation.
